top_choice_rationale: Cărtărescu (P002) has the most persuasive combination of an unmistakable voice, a large formal architecture carried by the sentence, and a body of work long enough to test sustained quality. On public descriptions, Blinding and Solenoid change the structure and narrating frame rather than restate one world, which answers the repetition worry as far as I can. That is an inference from public knowledge, not a comparison of passages. I have not independently verified any text. The achievement of the dense Romanian prose is exposed to translation loss, as are Michon's French and Wright's English idiom. Coverage of his poetry in translation is thin, so the case rests mainly on the prose, and the citation should say so. My margin over Michon (P001) is narrow and concerns breadth, not voice. Michon's sentence is arguably the more exact, and his consistency is a real form of sustained quality. Wright (P003) offers a formal departure rooted in a living oral practice, but her corpus is smaller and I cannot judge the relation of her English to Indigenous traditions from outside. Adonis (P004) is placed below the prose candidates because I cannot assess the Arabic line and no specialist assessment of the originals is in the record. That is a limit on my access, not a verdict on the poetry. No award (P000) is last, because each of the four named writers meets the standard of a serious oeuvre.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; my own practice in art, myth and fairy tale is context only, not evidence of merit, and I do not rely on my Lagerlöf biography for any preference
